nameStory: The Red-lined Panopoda gets its common name from the distinctive reddish lines that mark its forewings, creating striking linear patterns across its wings. The genus name 'Panopoda' comes from Greek words meaning 'all foot,' though the reason for this naming isn't entirely clear - it might refer to the moth's sturdy, well-developed legs.
description: The Red-lined Panopoda is a medium-sized moth in the diverse Erebidae family, which includes many of our most colorful night-flying moths. Its most notable feature is the series of reddish or rust-colored lines that run across its brown to grayish forewings, giving it a distinctive striped appearance. Like other moths in this family, it's primarily nocturnal and is often attracted to lights at night. Adults typically have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches.

idTips.label: Red wing lines
idTips.description: Look for distinctive reddish or rust-colored lines running across the forewings - these linear markings are the moth's signature feature and stand out clearly against the brown background

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Forewings are typically brown to grayish-brown with a somewhat matte finish, not shiny or iridescent like some other moths

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wingspan around 1.5-2 inches - about the size of a small butterfly but with the typical triangular moth wing shape

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies at night with the steady, direct flight typical of many Erebidae moths rather than the erratic flutter of smaller species

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are neither feathery nor clubbed, typical of many moth species in this family

habitat: Look for Red-lined Panopoda moths in deciduous and mixed forests where their caterpillar host plants grow - particularly areas with pignut hickory and northern red oak trees. They prefer mature woodlands and forest edges rather than open fields, and can be found from lowland forests up to moderate elevations throughout New England. Adults are most often encountered near outdoor lights or at moth sheets set up by naturalists.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin emerging in late spring, but this is typically not the peak flight period. Any moths seen would be at lights or occasionally disturbed during the day from resting spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season for adults, which are most active on warm, humid nights. This is the best time to spot them at porch lights or during moth surveys.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight period may extend into early fall. Caterpillars are actively feeding on hickory and oak leaves during this time, though they're well-camouflaged and rarely noticed.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil or leaf litter. No adults or caterpillars are visible during the cold months.

funFact: The caterpillars of Red-lined Panopoda moths are picky eaters that specifically target two of our most common forest trees - pignut hickory and northern red oak - yet despite feeding on these abundant trees, the adult moths are still uncommon enough that spotting one is considered a real treat for moth enthusiasts!
confusionNotes: Red-lined Panopoda moths could be confused with other brown moths in the Erebidae family, but the distinctive reddish lines across the forewings are usually diagnostic. Remember: 'Red lines, right ID' - if you see those rusty linear markings on brown wings, you've likely found your Panopoda.
contextualKnowledge: This moth belongs to the huge Erebidae family, which was only recently reorganized by scientists and used to be split among several different families. Many field guides published before 2010 might list this species under the old family name 'Noctuidae,' so don't be confused if you see different family names in older references.
compareHints: The Red-lined Panopoda is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our regional moths. Compared to other brown moths in the Erebidae family, it's distinguished by its specific pattern of reddish lines rather than spots, patches, or other markings. Most similar moths in this family have more complex wing patterns with multiple colors or eyespots, while the Red-lined Panopoda keeps it relatively simple with its characteristic linear design.
